'''AFC Bournemouth''' ({{IPAc-en|audio=en-uk-Bournemouth.ogg|ˈ|b|ɔːr|n|m|ə|θ}} {{respell|BORN|məth}}) is a professional [[association football|football]] club based in [[Kings Park, Boscombe]], a suburb of [[Bournemouth]], [[Dorset]], England. The club competes in the [[Premier League]], the top tier of [[English football league system|English football]]. Formed in 1899 as '''Boscombe''', the club adopted their current name in 1971. Nicknamed "The Cherries", and commonly referred to as '''Bournemouth''', they have played their home games at [[Dean Court]] since 1910. The club competed in regional football leagues before going up from the [[Hampshire League]] to the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]] in 1920. By then, known as '''Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic''', they were elected into the [[English Football League|Football League]] in 1923. They remained in the [[Football League Third Division South|Third Division South]] for 35 years, winning the [[Football League Third Division South Cup|Third Division South Cup]] in 1946. Placed in the newly reorganised [[Football League Third Division|Third Division]] in 1958, they suffered relegation in 1970, but would win an immediate promotion in 1970–71. Relegated back into the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] in 1975, Bournemouth were promoted again in 1981–82 and after lifting the [[EFL Trophy|Associate Members' Cup]] in [[1984 Associate Members' Cup Final|1984]] would go on to win the Third Division title in 1986–87. They spent three seasons in the second tier but entered [[Administration (British football)|administration]] in 1997 and ended up back in the fourth tier with relegation in 2002, though immediately gained promotion by winning the play-offs in [[2003 Football League Third Division play-off final |2003]]. Bournemouth entered administration for a second time and were relegated back into [[EFL League Two|League Two]] in 2008, but ended the year by appointing [[Eddie Howe]] as manager. Under Howe's stewardship, Bournemouth won three promotions in six years to win a place in the first tier of English football for the first time in their history. This was achieved with a second-place finish in League Two in 2009–10, a second-place finish in [[EFL League One|League One]] in 2012–13 and a [[EFL Championship|Championship]] title in 2014–15. The club remained in the [[Premier League]] for five seasons before suffering relegation in 2020, but they returned in 2022 as Championship runners-up, this time under the management of [[Scott Parker]]. Following their return to the top flight, the club achieved their highest league finish to date, by finishing 6th in 2025–26, thus earning European football and qualifying for the [[UEFA Europa League]] for the first time in their history, under the management of [[Andoni Iraola]]. ==History== ===Boscombe=== Although the exact date of the club's foundation is not known, there is proof that it was formed in the autumn of 1899 out of the remains of the older Boscombe St. John's Institute Football Club.{{cite web|title=AFC Bournemouth History |url=http://www.afcb.co.uk/club/club-history/ |date=12 May 2012 |access-date=25 June 2015 |location=Bournemouth |publisher=AFC Bournemouth |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626130115/http://www.afcb.co.uk/club/club-history/ |archive-date=26 June 2015}} The club was originally known as Boscombe Football Club. The first president was Mr. J. C. Nutt.The official Handbook of Bournemouth and Boscombe Athletic Football Club; ''Golden Jubilee 1899–1949'' In their first season, 1899–1900, Boscombe competed in the Bournemouth and District Junior League. They also played in the Hants Junior Cup. During the first two seasons, they played on a football pitch in Castlemain Avenue, Pokesdown. From their third season, the team played on a pitch in [[King's Park, Boscombe|King's Park]]. In the 1905–06 season, Boscombe graduated to senior amateur football.{{cite web |url=http://www.afcb.co.uk/club/club-history/ |date=24 May 2012 |title=AFCB Club History |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626130115/http://www.afcb.co.uk/club/club-history/ |archive-date=26 June 2015}} In 1910, the club was granted a long lease over some wasteland next to Kings Park as the club's football ground by local businessman J.E. Cooper-Dean. With their own ground, named Dean Court after the benefactor, the club continued to thrive, and dominated the local football scene. The same year the club signed its first professional player [[Baven Penton]].{{cite book |first1=Duncan |last1=Holley |first2=Gary |last2=Chalk |title=The Alphabet of the Saints |publisher=ACL & Polar Publishing |year=1992 |page=270 |isbn=0-9514862-3-3}} Around about this time, the club obtained their nickname "The Cherries". There are two leading explanations of how the club gained the nickname: from the cherry-red striped shirts that the team played in, and, perhaps less plausible, because Dean Court was built adjacent to the Cooper-Dean estate, which, it is believed, may have contained many cherry trees.{{Cite web |date=2023-02-25 |title=Ever Wonder why Bournemouth are nicknamed The Cherries? |url=https://www.nbcsports.com/soccer/news/ever-wonder-why-bournemouth-are-nicknamed-the-cherries |access-date=2024-09-06 |website=NBC Sports |language=en-US |archive-date=8 December 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241208020136/https://www.nbcsports.com/soccer/news/ever-wonder-why-bournemouth-are-nicknamed-the-cherries |url-status=live }} For the first time, during the 1913–14 season, the club competed in the [[FA Cup]]. The club's progress, however, was halted in 1914 with the outbreak of [[World War I]], and Boscombe returned to the [[Hampshire League]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} In 1920, the Third Division of the [[Football League]] was formed, and Boscombe were promoted to the [[Southern Football League|Southern League]], finding moderate success.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} [[File:Deancourt 14092013 vblackpool.jpg|thumbnail|[[Dean Court]]]] ===Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic=== To make the club more representative of the district, the name was changed to Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic Football Club in 1923. During the same year, the club was elected to the newly expanded [[Football League Third Division South|Third Division South]]. The first league match was at [[Swindon Town F.C.|Swindon Town]] on 25 August 1923, which Bournemouth lost 3–1. The first league game at Dean Court was also against Swindon, where Bournemouth gained their first league point after a 0–0 draw.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} Bournemouth struggled in the Football League but eventually established themselves as a Third Division club. Bournemouth remains on the records as the longest continuous members of the Third Division.{{Cite web |title=Football Club History Database – A F C Bournemouth |url=https://fchd.info/AFC-BOUR.HTM |access-date=2024-09-06 |website=fchd.info |archive-date=10 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240910022010/https://www.fchd.info/AFC-BOUR.HTM |url-status=live }} As a league club, Bournemouth had to wait until after the Second World War before winning their first trophy. This was accomplished as they beat [[Walsall F.C.|Walsall]] in the Third Division (South) Cup in the final at [[Stamford Bridge (stadium)|Stamford Bridge]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} ===AFC {{cite web |url=https://www.11v11.com/matches/hull-city-v-afc-bournemouth-24-may-1984-291534/ |title=Hull City v AFC Bournemouth, 24 May 1984 |website=11v11.com |publisher=AFS Enterprises |access-date=21 June 2020 |archive-date=21 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200621184945/https://www.11v11.com/matches/hull-city-v-afc-bournemouth-24-may-1984-291534/ |url-status=live }} Redknapp took Bournemouth into the second tier of the English league for the first time in their history as Third Division champions in 1987. After comfortably surviving in their first season in the Second Division, Bournemouth made a serious challenge for promotion to the top flight in the [[1988–89 in English football|1988–89 season]]; they ultimately fell away after a poor run late in the season, but their eventual finish of 12th place remained their highest-ever in the Football League until the [[2013–14 AFC Bournemouth season|2013–14 season]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} On 5 May 1990, the final day of the [[1989–90 in English football|1989–90 season]], [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] had the chance to win the Second Division and gain promotion into the First Division by beating Bournemouth at Dean Court. Some United fans had already caused trouble in the town during the morning and the atmosphere was tense as Leeds won the match by a single goal. Combined with the results of other matches, this meant that Leeds were promoted while Bournemouth were relegated. The violence and destruction by visitors to Bournemouth continued over the holiday weekend, causing more than £1 million worth of damage and injury to opposing fans and police officers.{{cite web |url=http://archive.bournemouthecho.co.uk/2004/5/5/67408.html |title=Bournemouth, Poole, Christchurch news, sports and jobs. Dorset and Hampshire what's on and leisure – Cherry-o Leeds! |website=Archive.bournemouthecho.co.uk |date=5 May 2004 |access-date=17 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100507170026/http://archive.bournemouthecho.co.uk/2004/5/5/67408.html |archive-date=7 May 2010}} The town's ''[[Bournemouth Daily Echo|Daily Echo]]'' newspaper reported that "spectators, including many young children, had to run to safety as missiles were hurled and riot police waded in to control the crowds." The matter was raised in Parliament by one of the town's MPs. Financially, the Leeds trouble affected the club for more than a decade, as Bournemouth were prevented by local police from staging home games on [[Bank holiday|Bank Holidays]] (traditionally a popular day for football) until a game against [[Shrewsbury Town F.C.|Shrewsbury Town]] on 21 April 2003.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} Redknapp remained at the club for two more seasons, both of which ended with the club falling three points short of the play-offs. However, mounting financial pressures caused him to resign his position at the end of the [[1991–92 in English football|1991–92 season]], and he subsequently re-joined former club [[West Ham United F.C.|West Ham United]] as a coach. He was replaced by [[Tony Pulis]], who built a much cheaper squad that could only manage two consecutive 17th-place finishes before Pulis walked out of the club, blaming financial pressures.{{citation needed|date=September 2018}} Bournemouth went the first few months of the [[1994–95 in English football|1994–95 season]] without a permanent manager in place, and a dreadful start saw them bottom of the table for much of the first half of the season. Despite a minor upturn in form when [[Mel Machin]] was appointed as manager, they looked highly unlikely to survive, given that there were five relegation spots in Division Two for that season due to league reconstruction. However, a late run of form combined with collapses by relegation rivals [[Cambridge United F.C.|Cambridge United]] and [[Plymouth Argyle F.C.|Plymouth Argyle]] saw them survive on the last day of the season by two points.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} Machin ultimately remained in charge for six years, most of which were marked by unremarkable mid-table finishes. The [[1998–99 in English football|1998–99 season]] proved to be arguably the highlight of his tenure, with the club making a serious playoff challenge for most of the season, but ultimately falling short and finishing seventh. However, a drop to 16th place in the [[1999–2000 AFC Bournemouth season|1999–2000 season]] followed by a poor start to the following season saw Machin removed from his position and given the role of director of football.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} ===Early 21st century=== [[Sean O'Driscoll]] was promoted from the coaching staff in place of Mel Machin at the start of the [[2000–01 AFC Bournemouth season|2000–01 season]]. In O'Driscoll's first season as manager, Bournemouth narrowly missed out on the Division Two playoffs but were relegated a year later in the new stadium (in the early part of the 2001–02 season, they played their home matches at [[Dorchester Town F.C.|Dorchester Town]]'s ground while their own stadium was being redeveloped). The board kept faith in O'Driscoll and they were rewarded with promotion via the Division Three playoffs in [[2002–03 in English football|2002–03]]. The club became the first to score five goals at the [[Millennium Stadium]] when they beat [[Lincoln City F.C.|Lincoln City]] 5–2 in the [[2002–03 in English football|2002–03]] Division Three play-off final with goals from [[Steve Fletcher]], [[Carl Fletcher (Welsh footballer)|Carl Fletcher]] (2), [[Stephen Purches]] and [[Garreth O'Connor]]. Under O'Driscoll, Bournemouth narrowly missed out on the play-offs for the [[2003–04 in English football|2003–04]] and [[2004–05 in English football|2004–05]] seasons, and just avoided relegation in the [[2005–06 in English football|2005–06]] season.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} Long-serving player [[James Hayter (footballer)|James Hayter]] scored the fastest league hat-trick in English Football League history during the [[2003–04 in English football|2003–04]] season. The Cherries were leading 3–0 against [[Wrexham F.C.|Wrexham]] thanks to goals from Stephen Purches, [[Warren Cummings]] and [[Warren Feeney]] when Hayter was brought onto the field as a substitute. With 86 minutes gone, Hayter managed to net three goals in the space of two minutes and 21 seconds, making the final score 6–0 to Bournemouth.{{Cite web |title=Records |url=https://www.efl.com/about-the-efl/history/records/ |access-date=2024-06-03 |website=efl.com |archive-date=3 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603143418/https://www.efl.com/about-the-efl/history/records/ |url-status=live }} In September 2006, with the team in eighth in the League, Sean O'Driscoll left to become manager of [[Doncaster Rovers F.C.|Doncaster Rovers]]. He was replaced by [[Kevin Bond (English footballer)|Kevin Bond]].{{Cite web |date=2006-10-12 |title=Ex-Saints coach unveiled as Cherries boss |url=https://www.dailyecho.co.uk/sport/966645.ex-saints-coach-unveiled-as-cherries-boss/ |access-date=2024-06-03 |website=dailyecho.co.uk}} ===Decline and administration (2008–2009)=== In February 2008, Bournemouth were forced into administration, suffering a ten-point deduction which put them in relegation trouble. Bournemouth had debts of around £4 million and almost went out of business.{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/teams/b/bournemouth/7233678.stm |title=Cherries go into administration |website=BBC Sport |date=8 February 2008 |access-date=17 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080210215154/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/b/bournemouth/7233678.stm |archive-date=10 February 2008 |url-status=live}} The off-field uncertainty continued throughout the season, with only one, ultimately unsuccessful, bid for the club accepted,{{cite web |url=http://world.afcb.co.uk/page/NewsDetail/0,,10324~1280796,00.html |title=3 April Press conference transcript |website=AFC Bournemouth |access-date=17 May 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180404134434/http://world.afcb.co.uk/page/NewsDetail/0,,10324~1280796,00.html |archive-date=4 April 2018}} and the club ended the season being relegated to [[EFL League Two|League Two]].{{Cite web |title=Football Club History Database – A F C Bournemouth |url=https://fchd.info/AFC-BOUR.HTM |access-date=2024-09-06 |website=fchd.info}} Ahead of the [[2008–09 in English football|2008–09 season]], the team's future in the Football League was put into doubt when the league threatened to block Bournemouth's participation in League Two, due to problems with the club's continuing administration and change in ownership. The league ordered both Bournemouth and [[Rotherham United F.C.|Rotherham United]] to demonstrate that they could fulfil all of their fixtures and find a way out of administration,[https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/aug/06/rotherham.bournemouth Troubled League Two clubs on the brink] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170305003433/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/aug/06/rotherham.bournemouth |date=5 March 2017 }} ''The Guardian'', 6 August 2008 eventually allowing the club to compete with a 17-point penalty for failing to follow the Football League insolvency rules. The new company was also ordered to pay unsecured creditors the amount offered at the time of the original [[Trading while insolvent#Company voluntary agreement|CVA]] (around ten pence in the pound) within two years.[https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/aug/07/bournemouth.leaguetwofootball Bournemouth hit by 17 point penalty] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170305003419/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/aug/07/bournemouth.leaguetwofootball |date=5 March 2017 }} ''The Guardian'', 7 August 2008 Early into the season, manager Bond was sacked and was replaced by former player [[Jimmy Quinn (Northern Irish footballer)|Jimmy Quinn]], who would himself leave the club only a few months later.[http://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/4013110.QUINN_AND_CHERRIES_PART_COMPANY Quinn and Cherries Part Company] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120304065322/http://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/4013110.QUINN_AND_CHERRIES_PART_COMPANY/ |date=4 March 2012 }} ''Bournemouth Daily Echo'', 31 December 2008 Former player [[Eddie Howe]] took over as manager with the club still ten points adrift at the bottom of the league and initially on a caretaker basis, becoming the youngest manager in the Football League at the age of 31.{{cite news |url=http://www.skysports.com/story/0,19528,11750_4817560,00.html |title=Howe handed permanent role |date=19 January 2009 |access-date=19 January 2009 |website=Sky Sports |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090602062338/http://www.skysports.com/story/0,19528,11750_4817560,00.html |archive-date=2 June 2009 |url-status=live}} At the end of 2008, it was announced that local businessman Adam Murray had completed the purchase of 50% of the club's shares from previous chairman, Paul Baker. However, in January 2009, Murray missed the deadline to buy Baker's shares.[http://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/4013023.UPDATED__CLUB_CONFIRMS_BAKER_BUY_OUT Club Confirms Baker Buy-Out] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120304065441/http://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/4013023.UPDATED__CLUB_CONFIRMS_BAKER_BUY_OUT/ |date=4 March 2012 }} ''Bournemouth Daily Echo'', 31 December 2008 In the final home game of the 2008–09 season, the Cherries guaranteed their Football League status by beating [[Grimsby Town F.C.|Grimsby Town]] 2–1 with a winning goal ten minutes from time by Bournemouth's Steve Fletcher, sparking celebrations after an ending to "The Great Escape." They finished their season with a 4–0 victory at [[Morecambe F.C.|Morecambe]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} In June 2009, a consortium including Adam Murray finally took over Bournemouth. The consortium included Jeff Mostyn, former vice-chairman Steve Sly, Neill Blake and former [[Dorchester Town]] chairman [[Eddie Mitchell]].{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} ===Rise to the Premier League (2009–2015)=== Howe's first full season in charge brought success as Bournemouth finished second in League Two to earn promotion with two games to spare. Howe left the club for [[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]] during the following season; his successor, another former Bournemouth player, [[Lee Bradbury]], led Bournemouth to the League One play-offs. The two-legged semi-final against [[Huddersfield Town F.C.|Huddersfield Town]] finished 3–3 after extra time, and Huddersfield went through the final by winning the penalty shoot-out 4–2. Bradbury was unable to lead Bournemouth to another promotion challenge in the [[2011–12 Football League One]], placing 11th after a season of indifferent results, and was replaced by youth team coach [[Paul Groves (footballer)|Paul Groves]] for the final games of the season.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} Groves remained in charge at the start of the [[2012–13 AFC Bournemouth season|2012–13 season]], only to be sacked in October 2012 following a start which left the club near the bottom of the table. Eddie Howe returned as manager, and not only did he pull the club away from their early-season relegation battle, they achieved promotion to the [[EFL Championship|Championship]], returning to the second-tier of English football for the first time since 1990. The club also revealed a new club crest.[http://www.football-shirts.co.uk/fans/afc-bournemouth-launch-new-crest_21507.AFC Bournemouth Launch New Crest]{{Dead link|date=April 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ''Football-shirts.co.uk'', 15 July 2013 After a promising start to life in the Championship, the club was handed a fourth Round [[FA Cup]] tie with [[Premier League]] club [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] which ended in a 2–0 loss. Bournemouth finished their first season back in the Championship in tenth place, their highest ever position in the Football League.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} On 25 October 2014, Bournemouth won 8–0 away at [[St Andrew's (stadium)|St. Andrew's]] against [[Birmingham City F.C.|Birmingham City]]. It was the first time that the Cherries had ever scored eight goals in a league game and their largest winning margin in the league (not counting a 10–0 win over [[Northampton Town F.C.|Northampton Town]] in September 1939, which was discounted after the league was abandoned due to the Second World War).{{cite web |year=2014 |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/0/football/29669693 |title=Managerless Birmingham City suffered a humiliating defeat as Bournemouth scored eight goals at St Andrew's |website=BBC Sport |access-date=25 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141026213420/http://www.bbc.com/sport/0/football/29669693 |archive-date=26 October 2014| url-status =live}} The club followed up this success with a 2–1 victory over [[Premier League]] side [[West Bromwich Albion F.C.|West Bromwich Albion]] in the League Cup, reaching the quarter-finals of the competition for the first time. Bournemouth were again drawn against Liverpool but lost 3–1. The club spent most of the [[2014–15 AFC Bournemouth season|2014–15 season]] near the top of the table, and a 3–0 win away at [[Charlton Athletic F.C.|Charlton Athletic]] on the final day of the season was enough to clinch the Championship title and a first-ever promotion to the top flight of English football.{{cite news |title=Gallery: All the incredible pictures as Cherries are crowned champions of Football League |url=http://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/12928783.GALLERY__All_the_incredible_pictures_as_Cherries_are_crowned_champions_of_Football_League/ |newspaper=Bournemouth Echo |access-date=2 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150505021053/http://www.bournemouthecho.co.uk/news/12928783.GALLERY__All_the_incredible_pictures_as_Cherries_are_crowned_champions_of_Football_League/ |archive-date=5 May 2015|url-status=live}} ===First Premier League era (2015–2020)=== In Bournemouth's [[2015–16 AFC Bournemouth season|first season]] in the Premier League, the team was beset by a number of crippling injuries, including to [[Callum Wilson (English footballer)|Callum Wilson]], star striker from the previous season. AFC Bournemouth (  BORN-məth) is a professional football club based in Kings Park, Boscombe, a suburb of Bournemouth, Dorset, England. The club competes in the Premier League, the top tier of English football. Formed in 1899 as Boscombe, the club adopted their current name in 1971. Nicknamed "The Cherries", and commonly referred to as Bournemouth, they have played their home games at Dean Court since 1910. 
The club competed in regional football leagues before going up from the Hampshire League to the Southern League in 1920. By then, known as Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic, they were elected into the Football League in 1923. They remained in the Third Division South for 35 years, winning the Third Division South Cup in 1946. Placed in the newly reorganised Third Division in 1958, they suffered relegation in 1970, but would win an immediate promotion in 1970–71. Relegated back into the Fourth Division in 1975, Bournemouth were promoted again in 1981–82 and after lifting the Associate Members' Cup in 1984 would go on to win the Third Division title in 1986–87. They spent three seasons in the second tier but entered administration in 1997 and ended up back in the fourth tier with relegation in 2002, though immediately gained promotion by winning the play-offs in 2003.
Bournemouth entered administration for a second time and were relegated back into League Two in 2008, but ended the year by appointing Eddie Howe as manager. Under Howe's stewardship, Bournemouth won three promotions in six years to win a place in the first tier of English football for the first time in their history. This was achieved with a second-place finish in League Two in 2009–10, a second-place finish in League One in 2012–13 and a Championship title in 2014–15. The club remained in the Premier League for five seasons before suffering relegation in 2020, but they returned in 2022 as Championship runners-up, this time under the management of Scott Parker. Following their return to the top flight, the club achieved their highest league finish to date, by finishing 6th in 2025–26, thus earning European football and qualifying for the UEFA Europa League for the first time in their history, under the management of Andoni Iraola.
